title: The Mark of a Criminal Record
text:
In 2001 Devah Pager, a graduate student in sociology at the University of Wisconsin, sent pairs of young men to apply for real entry-level jobs in Milwaukee. The men were college students chosen to be similar in appearance and manner, and they were given matching fictional resumes. One pair was white and the other pair was Black.

Within each pair, the men took turns presenting a criminal record: a felony drug conviction and eighteen months in prison. Otherwise they applied in the same way to the same employers, in hundreds of applications in total, and the researchers recorded which applicants were called back.

Among white applicants, 34 percent without a record were called back, compared with 17 percent of those with a record. Among Black applicants, 14 percent without a record were called back, and only 5 percent of those with a record. A criminal record cut a man's chances roughly in half, and for Black applicants the effect was even larger. Most striking, white applicants with a prison record were called back at least as often as Black applicants with a clean record. Pager concluded that a criminal record, and race, act as powerful marks that close doors before an applicant can show what he can do.
lesson: Labels like a past record can close doors before a person can show who they are now. When you can, give people a chance to be judged on what they do today.
source: Pager, D. (2003). The mark of a criminal record. American Journal of Sociology, 108(5), 937-975.
